name: Memory inhibition
statement: Recalling one member of a category is claimed to inhibit its unretrieved neighbours, leaving them harder to recall later than items from categories nobody practised.
meaning: The claim rests on one task. Participants study category and exemplar pairs, such as fruit orange and fruit banana. They then practise retrieving half the exemplars from half the categories, cued by the category name and a word stem. A final test asks for everything studied. Three item types come out of this. Practised items are labelled Rp+, unpractised items from practised categories Rp-, and items from untouched categories Nrp. Rp+ items are recalled best, which is the ordinary benefit of retrieval. The result the literature is built on is that Rp- items are recalled worse than Nrp items, so retrieving orange costs banana. Anderson, Bjork and Bjork read that cost as active suppression of the competitor. The rival reading is blocking by the strengthened item. Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli and Storm describe the two camps as inhibition accounts against non-inhibitory accounts such as strength-based competition and blocking. The distinction matters because inhibition is a claim about the memory itself, while competition is a claim about what happens at the moment of the test. Storm and Levy, writing for the inhibition side, set out what that account does and does not claim. Its proponents do not hold that non-inhibitory mechanisms cannot cause the forgetting. Their claim is narrower, that many features of it resist explanation by purely non-inhibitory processes. This entry covers the retrieval-practice paradigm. The think/no-think task and directed forgetting sit under motivated forgetting, entry 215.

origin.who: Michael C. Anderson, Robert A. Bjork and Elizabeth L. Bjork
origin.where: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
origin.note: The paper names the effect retrieval-induced forgetting and argues that suppression, not strength-dependent competition, produces it. Its own framing is that three assumptions of existing competition models already imply the effect, and that the data violate the strength-dependence assumption among them. The article states that it appears on University Microfilms as part of Anderson's UCLA doctoral dissertation.

evidence: Anderson, Bjork and Bjork ran three experiments on UCLA psychology students, 36 in the first, 48 in the second and 64 in the third. Experiment 1 gave eight six-item categories, four built from strong exemplars and four from weak ones. Three exemplars from two strong and two weak categories were then retrieved three times each. A 20-minute gap filled with an unrelated task came before category-cued recall. Practised items were recalled at 73.6% against a baseline of 48.4%, F(1, 32) = 136.9, p < .0001, and their unpractised neighbours at 37.5%, F(1, 32) = 30.3, p < .0001. The loss was not spread evenly. Strong unpractised items fell from 56.0% to 40.3%, weak ones only from 41.0% to 34.7%, which runs against the prediction that weak items suffer most. Both losses were reliable, F(1, 32) = 27.4 for strong items and F(1, 32) = 4.5 for weak ones. What differed was their size, not whether they happened. Experiment 2 added a two-letter stem at test and fixed the output order so that unpractised items could be tested before practised ones. Averaged over position the impairment was not reliable, 68.8% against 73%, F(1, 40) = 2.3, p = .13. It held for strong categories alone, 74.7% against 82.7%, F(1, 40) = 7.2, p < .01. Weak categories showed 62.9% against 62.7%. Testing the strong unpractised items first still cost 7.6 points, which is the paper's evidence that the damage outlasts the practice phase. Experiment 3 crossed the strength of practised and unpractised items across four groups of 16. Impairment tracked the strength of the competitor, 53.9% against 63.4%, F(1, 60) = 7.6, p < .01. It did not track the strength of the practised item, where strong and weak practice differed by 2.9 points against 0.3 points, F(1, 60) < 1. Weak unpractised items were if anything helped, 45.1% against 38.8%, F(1, 60) = 3.3, p = .07. Murayama and colleagues later pooled the literature. Searching PsycINFO and Web of Science for work published before August 2012, they identified 194 papers, kept 143, and drew 759 effect sizes from 512 samples. The weighted mean was g = 0.35, 95% CI [0.32, 0.38], with Q(511) = 1381.2 and I-squared of 63.0%. A separate analysis of raw recall rates, restricted to the 221 samples that printed them, put the gap between the two item types at 8.5 percentage points, CI [7.4, 9.6].

replication.headline: The forgetting itself is solid, at g = 0.35 across 512 samples, and about half of it is competition at the moment of the test rather than damage done during practice.
replication.detail: Rowland, Bates and DeLosh ran the closest thing to a direct replication. Seventy-two undergraduates gave 45% recall for baseline items against 41% for unpractised neighbours, t(71) = 2.59, p = 0.01, d = 0.31. A second experiment on 140 people recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk gave 50% against 42%, t(139) = 4.51, p < 0.01, d = 0.38. Both cleared the benchmark they had set in advance using Simonsohn's method, a d of 0.26 derived from the original sample size. Their third experiment copied Anderson and Spellman's independent-cue procedure on 67 people and found nothing. The standard comparison gave t(66) = 0.92, p = 0.36. The cue-independent comparison gave d = -0.05, 95% CI [-0.36, 0.27]. By their own criterion that is an uninformative failure rather than an informative one. Murayama and colleagues' meta-analysis puts the same split on a larger base. Studies that let practised items be recalled first before the unpractised ones report g = 0.50, CI [0.45, 0.55], k = 256. Studies that control that output order report g = 0.22, CI [0.19, 0.26], k = 280, a difference of Q(1) = 77.0, p < .01. The raw-recall analysis rests on a smaller set and splits the same way, 10.9 percentage points across 142 samples and 4.5 across 90. Cue-independent designs, the ones meant to show that the item rather than the cue was damaged, give g = 0.16, CI [0.09, 0.24], k = 67. Restudying items instead of retrieving them produces no forgetting at all, g = 0.07, CI [-0.03, 0.17], k = 17, which is the strongest single result in the inhibition account's favour. Retrieving the category name from the exemplar should not pit exemplars against each other, yet it produces g = 0.37, CI [0.04, 0.71], k = 7. That is the strongest single result against inhibition. Those seven samples disagree with each other at I-squared of 73.9%. Where the theory is tested outside recall, the record is worse. Potter, Huszar and Huber reanalysed Wimber and colleagues' 2015 imaging study, whose key interaction was reported at p = .041. That interaction depended on scoring missing responses as errors rather than as guesses or as missing. Treated either of the other two ways, the difference in forgetting between competitors and targets was not reliable. They then ran the behavioural paradigm twice, on 22 analysed participants and on 48 in a pre-registered replication, and found no forgetting at all.

study.cite: Rowland, C. A., Bates, L. E., & DeLosh, E. L. (2014). On the reliability of retrieval-induced forgetting. Frontiers in Psychology, 5, 1343.

limits: The effect and its explanation are not the same question, and this page grades only the first. Whether inhibition causes the forgetting is open, and the arguments for competition come from Raaijmakers and Jakab and from Jonker, Seli and MacLeod. Raaijmakers and Jakab tested the interference-dependence and retrieval-specificity assumptions and concluded that the results fit competition at the time of the later test. Jonker, Seli and MacLeod propose that the practice phase shifts the internal context. A category cue at test then reinstates the practice context for practised categories and the study context for the rest. Unpractised neighbours lose a reinstatement benefit their baselines keep. Their three experiments used two different context manipulations, with 30 people to a group in the first two and 164 in the third. Experiment 1 was a plain extra-study replication, which produced no forgetting. Experiment 2 shifted context with an imagination task between study and extra study. Forgetting then appeared where inhibition predicts none, and was abolished again when participants were guided back to the study context. Experiment 3 paired study and practice with different video clips and cued the final test with one of them. The practice video gave forgetting, t(81) = 6.49, d = 0.72, and the study video removed it, t(81) = 1.63, p = .11. A previous version of this entry said all three experiments used video clips, which the paper does not support. Cue-dependent forgetting, entry 253, is the wider literature the context account draws on. Murayama and colleagues' meta-analysis read here is the accepted manuscript posted at the University of Reading, not the published version. Raaijmakers and Jakab's two papers were read from the first author's own page at Amsterdam, the review as a publisher proof and the shorter piece as an author manuscript. Neither is certified identical to its published version. Rowland and colleagues derive their 0.26 benchmark from Anderson, Bjork and Bjork's Experiment 2, which they give as 36 people, though that experiment ran 48 and the first ran 36. They print d without an interval for the two experiments that found the effect, and print one only for the cue-independent comparison that did not. Delay is unsettled. Samples tested a day or more after practice give g = 0.09, CI [-0.07, 0.25], k = 38. Dropping the studies that used prose passages raises that to g = 0.40, CI [0.20, 0.61], k = 21. No multi-laboratory replication of the retrieval-practice paradigm was located in searches of Crossref, the OSF registration listings and the open web on 21 September 2026. Registered single-laboratory work does exist, and Potter and colleagues' third study is one. The registered multisite effort in the wider memory-inhibition literature is the Memory Control Consortium's think/no-think replication, which tests a different task and is covered under motivated forgetting, entry 215.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating a replicated effect as a replicated mechanism. Murayama and colleagues found the forgetting across 512 samples and still describe the theoretical picture as mixed, and their own summary is that the moderators largely favour inhibition while some of them do not. The second error is quoting the headline size. Roughly half the effect in the published record comes from practised items being recalled first at the final test and crowding out the rest, and once that is controlled the gap is 4.5 percentage points. The third is reading the original paper as showing that remembering damages whatever it competes with. It did not: weak exemplars lost least in Experiment 1, were unaffected in Experiment 2, and were marginally helped in Experiment 3, and the authors' own conclusion is that the competitor's strength, not the practised item's, decides who suffers. Their weak-item loss in Experiment 1 was real, so the claim that weak competitors escape unharmed overstates the paper in the other direction. The fourth is using the paradigm as a personality measure. Jonker, Seli and MacLeod call the scoring of special populations on inhibitory ability with this task premature. They point at a published claim that inhibitory processes in memory are impaired in schizophrenia as the kind of inference it licenses. The fifth is merging this task with deliberate suppression. Retrieval-induced forgetting is a by-product of trying to remember something else, and nobody in the experiment is trying to forget anything. The think/no-think task, where people are told to keep a memory out of mind, is a separate literature with a weaker record, and this atlas keeps it under motivated forgetting, entry 215.
